Source: Mock E · Paper 2 · Vignette 6

Belle operates predominantly in the UK. Lee gathers the information about EUR/GBP exchange rates (amount of EUR per 1 GBP) in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1

#  | EUR/GBP Exchange Rate

16 November, most recent year | 1.186

31 December, most recent year | 1.176

18 January, current year | 1.193

Lee notes that Belle purchased inventory for GBP 500,000 from an unaffiliated UK company on 16 November of the most recent year. The transaction was settled on 18 January of the current year.

Belle uses the current rate method to translate its subsidiaries' financial statements. In contrast, Belle's primary competitor uses the temporal method to translate its subsidiaries' financial statements. Lee considers how each company should report its cumulative translation adjustment under the method used.

questions.q: As a result of the inventory purchase, Belle should recognize a foreign currency transaction loss of:
options: EUR 5,000 in the most recent year.
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Belle would recognize an unrealized foreign currency gain, not loss, of EUR 593,000 – EUR 588,000 = EUR 5,000 at the end of the most recent year.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this represents the net foreign currency loss from transaction date to settlement date. Belle owed GBP 500,000, which would cost EUR 593,000 (GBP 500,000 × EUR/GBP 1.186). At the settlement date, Belle would pay EUR 596,500 (GBP 500,000 × EUR/GBP 1.193). The total foreign currency loss in the current year is EUR 3,500 (EUR 596,500 – EUR 593,000).

questions.q: Belle should report its cumulative translation adjustment as:
options: a component of other operating income.
a separate component of stockholders' equity.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this represents a potential treatment of a foreign currency transaction and not a translation adjustment. The two most common treatments (of foreign currency transaction gains and losses, not translation adjustments) are either (1) as a component of other operating income/expense or (2) as a component of non-operating income. Belle uses the current rate method, and when the current rate method is used, the cumulative translation adjustment needed to keep the translated balance sheet in balance is reported as a separate component of stockholders’ equity.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Belle uses the current rate method and this represents treatment under the temporal method. Under both international and US accounting standards, when the temporal method is used, the translation adjustment needed to keep the translated balance sheet in balance is reported as a gain or loss in net income.
It also represents a potential treatment of a foreign currency transaction, not a translation adjustment. The two most common treatments (of foreign currency transaction gains and losses, not translation adjustments) are either (1) as a component of other operating income/expense or (2) as a component of non-operating income.
C. Correct.

Source: Mock F · Paper 1 · Vignette 11

Karl Reinke, a research analyst, is examining the financial statements of Argon plc, a UK-based company that reports under IFRS. Argon's primary competitors are US-based companies that report under US GAAP. On 1 January of the current year, Argon purchased a 40% non-controlling interest in Xenon plc for GBP 500 million. The book values of the assets and liabilities were equal to their fair values except for inventory, which was undervalued by GBP 5 million, and equipment, which was undervalued by GBP 10 million. Xenon uses the FIFO inventory valuation method and depreciates all of its equipment using the straight-line method. The equipment has an estimated remaining useful life of ten years with no residual value. Reinke estimates that Xenon will report net income of GBP 60 million and will not declare any dividends for the current year.

Argon also acquired an 80% controlling interest in Radon plc in the current year, and has elected to use the partial goodwill option for recognizing goodwill when consolidating Radon.

questions.q: The estimated amount of Argon's investment in Xenon at the end of the current year should be:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the depreciation for the undervalued equipment is treated as though it was overvalued (500.0 + 24.0 – 2.0 + 0.4 = 522.4).
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the deduction for the inventory sold under the FIFO valuation method is omitted from the calculation (500.0 + 24.0 – 0.4 = 523.6).

questions.q: When consolidating Radon, Argon's D/E ratio at the end of the current year would be:
options: lower than if it used the method of its primary competitors.
the same as if it used the method of its primary competitors.
higher than if it used the method of its primary competitors.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because total shareholders' equity is lower under the partial goodwill method, thereby increasing the debt-to-equity ratio. Total debt is the same under both methods.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because total shareholders' equity is lower under the partial goodwill method, thereby increasing the debt-to-equity ratio. Total debt is the same under both methods. 
C. Correct.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock F · Paper 2 · Vignette 6

Joanne Gordon is a buy-side analyst covering the banking and insurance sectors.

Gordon first analyzes the liquidity of Grand Bank. She reviews the information (in $ millions) from the bank's most recent annual report in Exhibit 1 and calculates its liquidity coverage ratio.

Exhibit 1

High-quality liquid assets | 400

Net cash outflows | 300

High-quality liquid assets in excess of net cash outflows | 100

Total available stable funding | 1,300

Total required stable funding | 1,100

Bronx Insurance has two share-based compensation plans: (1) a restricted stock unit (RSU) plan for employees; and (2) executive stock options. Settlement for the RSUs is made at the end of each year. On the grant date at the beginning of the first year, the share price was $6.00 per RSU. At the end of the second year, the share price was $5.00 per RSU. The CEO has vested stock options equivalent to 10% of the company's current outstanding shares. Gordon forecasts a net loss for Bronx Insurance during the second year of the RSU plan.

questions.q: The liquidity coverage ratio for Grand Bank is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the calculation uses the high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) in excess of net cash outflows in the numerator instead of total high-quality liquid assets as required.
LCR = HQLA in excess of net cash outflows/Net cash outflows = 100/300 ≈ 33%
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the value for the net stable funding ratio. 
Net stable funding ratio = Total available stable funding/Total required stable funding
= 1,300/1,100 ≈ 118%
C. Correct.

questions.q: As a result of the employee RSU plan and executive stock options, Gordon's forecasted value for diluted EPS of the second year of the RSU plan should be:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because when EPS is positive, unvested RSUs are added to shares outstanding balance, resulting in a lower diluted EPS than basic EPS. The options would be excluded from the calculation as they are anti-dilutive: exercise is uneconomic for the holder, and if they were exercised, fewer shares would be issued upon their exercise than would be repurchased with the resulting cash received, reducing shares outstanding and increasing EPS.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because diluted EPS cannot exceed basic EPS, so companies that report a net loss will report the same basic and diluted shares outstanding.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock B · Paper 1 · Vignette 1

Singh would like to take advantage of the under-leveraged balance sheet of Axiom while ensuring that the company's current shareholders retain control. Singh considers what corporate actions could achieve these objectives.

Division B generated an EBITDA of $10.8 million last year and is valued at 6.0x EV/EBITDA. Division B has two segments:

A wholesale segment which contributed 20% to the division's EBITDA. Comparable wholesale retailers are valued at 7.0x EV/EBITDA.

A consumer segment which contributed 80% to the division's EBITDA. Comparable consumer retailers are valued at 5.1x EV/EBITDA.

Singh evaluates if spinning off Division B's wholesale segment would have a material impact on shareholder value, which she defines as a change in shareholder value of greater than 5%.

questions.q: Which of the following corporate actions would best meet Singh's objectives?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. A reorganization is a court-supervised restructuring of an insolvent company. Axiom is under-leveraged and Singh wants to add debt, so this does not fit.
B. Incorrect. An LBO is an acquirer-led strategy that uses a lot of debt to buy a target. Singh wants the current shareholders to keep control, so this does not fit.
C. Correct. A dividend recapitalization restructures the mix from equity to debt through debt-financed dividends or repurchases. It replaces expensive equity with cheaper debt, does not dilute shareholders' stakes and can increase value to shareholders.

questions.q: Based on Singh's analysis, spinning off the wholesale segment for Division B would lead to:
options: a material decrease in shareholder wealth.
no material impact on shareholder wealth.
a material increase in shareholder wealth.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Sum of the parts: 7.0 × 20% × 10.8 = 15.120 and 5.1 × 80% × 10.8 = 44.064, total 59.184. Division B is valued at 6 × 10.8 = 64.800, so the change is (59.184 − 64.800)/64.800 = −8.7%, a material decrease (the market values synergies between the segments).
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: this averages the two multiples ((7.0 + 5.1)/2 = 6.05), giving 65.340 and a change of only +0.8%.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this swaps the multiples (5.1 × 20% × 10.8 + 7.0 × 80% × 10.8 = 71.496), giving +10.3%.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock C · Paper 1 · Vignette 8

Feldcroft is considering the purchase of a new corporate helicopter to access remote construction sites. Traver evaluates a proposal for a 10-year lease with payments of $125,000 at the end of each month. The helicopter has a fair value of $15 million, and the lessor would incur a direct cost of $750,000 at the beginning of the lease. The residual value of the helicopter at the end of the lease is expected to be $8,700,000. Feldcroft has an unsecured incremental borrowing rate of 8%.

Feldcroft has operations in Country A, an emerging market that represents 10% of the company's revenue. To estimate the equity risk premium that should be used in calculating Feldcroft's cost of equity, Traver uses the country spread model with no adjustment for the relative volatility of Country A equity and bond returns. The current US equity risk premium is 5.94% and 10-year US Treasury bonds yield 3.50%. Country A recently issued a 10-year bond denominated in local currency that yields 7.55% and a 10-year bond denominated in US dollars that yields 5.15%.

Feldcroft is considering acquiring a construction company that has sales of $7.00 per share. To estimate a fair takeover value for this target company, Traver uses comparable transaction analysis with equal weights on three transactions, as shown in Exhibit 1. He notes that Feldcroft's current price-to-sales (P/S) ratio is 1.35 and that transactions in the construction industry take place at an average takeover premium of 8%.

Exhibit 1

# Variable | Acquired Company 1 | Acquired Company 2 | Acquired Company 3

Sales per share | $6.30 | $12.98 | $9.01

P/S ratio at acquisition price | 1.78 | 1.84 | 1.63

Finally, Traver prepares a pro forma income statement reflecting the acquisition of the target construction company. He assumes the acquisition would generate cost synergies and be funded with new debt, which would include refinancing the target company's existing debt. After separating depreciation and amortization from operating expenses, Traver models selected pro forma income statement balances as follows:

Interest expense: Add interest expense from the new debt issuance to the target company's current interest expense

Operating expenses: Add cost synergies to and subtract cost dis-synergies from combined operating expenses

Depreciation and amortization expense: Add amortization of acquired intangible assets to combined depreciation and amortization expense

questions.q: The implied annual interest cost of the helicopter lease is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response does not include Feldcroft's direct costs as part of the cash flows of the lease. Using a calculator, the implied interest cost is calculated as follows:
Payment (PMT) = $125,000
Present value (PV) = –$15,000,000
Number of payments (N) = 120 (10 years × 12 monthly payments)
Future value (FV) = $8,700,000
Solve for interest rate (i) = 0.5921% per month
Implied annual interest rate = 0.5921% × 12 = 7.1049% ≈ 7.10%
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response assumes the lease cost will be based on Feldcroft's unsecured incremental borrowing rate. However, the implied interest cost of the lease is based on the cash flows of the lease itself and is calculated independently from the unsecured incremental borrowing rate.

questions.q: Based on the country spread model, the equity risk premium that should be used in calculating Feldcroft's cost of equity is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response uses Country A's 10-year bond denominated in local currency instead of the USD-denominated 10-year bond. This response incorrectly calculates the equity risk premium as:
ERP = 5.94% + [10% × (7.55% – 3.50%)]
ERP = 6.345% ≈ 6.35%
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response does not adjust Feldcroft's equity risk premium (ERP) for the level of exposure to Country A. This response incorrectly calculates the equity risk premium as:
ERP = 5.94% + (5.15% – 3.50%)
ERP = 7.59%

questions.q: Based on comparable transaction analysis, the fair takeover value per share of the target construction company is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response applies Feldcroft's P/S ratio of 1.35 instead of the mean P/S ratio of the comparable transactions (1.75). Given the target company's sales per share of $7.00:
Fair takeover value per share = Sales per share × Feldcroft's P/S ratio
= $7.00 × 1.35
= $9.45
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response adds the 8% average takeover premium in the construction industry, which is double-counting as the premium is already embedded in the comparable transaction multiples. Given the target company's sales per share of $7.00:
Fair takeover value per share = Sales per share × Mean P/S of comparable transactions × (1 + Average industry takeover premium)
Mean P/S of comparable transactions = (1.78 + 1.84 + 1.63) / 3 = 1.75
Fair takeover value per share = $7.00 × 1.75 × (1 + 8%) = $13.23

questions.q: Which of the following balances on the pro forma income statement does Traver most likely model correctly?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Traver double counts interest expense on the target's pre-acquisition debt, which would be refinanced as part of the new debt issuance associated with the acquisition. In addition, to the extent Feldcroft has any pre-acquisition debt (which is not stated in the vignette), Traver also omits interest expense related to that debt.
1. Start with current acquirer interest expense.
2. Add increased interest from new debt issuance and revised interest rate.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because cost synergies should be subtracted from, not added to, operating expenses, and cost dis-synergies should be added to, not subtracted from, operating expenses. 
1. Combine acquirer and target operating expenses.
2. Subtract cost synergies or add the cost of incompatible activities (dis-synergies).
C. Correct.

When calculating a weighted average estimated price, she assigns a weight of 50% to the price-to-sales (P/S) multiple, and a 25% weight to each of the other two multiples. She considers the acquisition to be fairly priced if the price paid is within $1 of her estimate on a per share basis.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock E · Paper 1 · Vignette 2

Next, Sylvester estimates the company's current cost of capital. To estimate Palmco's cost of equity, Sylvester initially considers using a historical approach with arithmetic mean returns and a short-term government bill rate as a proxy for the risk-free rate. However, Sylvester identifies a number of disadvantages with this approach.

Palmco's CEO, Jacky Westerholm, approaches Sylvester with a proposal that Palmco acquire Spritz Ltd. Spritz is a privately held drinks company that specializes in alcoholic seltzers, a fast-growing segment of the beverage market that Palmco has yet to enter. Not only will Spritz provide Palmco with a fast-growing revenue stream, it will also provide synergies in the form of cost savings from consolidating production facilities. To provide a quick estimate of the price that Palmco should expect to pay to acquire Spritz, Sylvester gathers information about two comparable transactions, both of which completed in the last two years. Exhibit 1 shows the transaction price per share for each comparable company, along with various per share metrics which are given equal weights in Sylvester's analysis.

Exhibit 1

#  | Company 1 | Company 2 | Spritz

Transaction share price (£) | 10.55 | 35.60 | 

Earnings per share (£) | 0.52 | 1.36 | 3.24

Book value per share (£) | 3.15 | 10.05 | 15.62

Palmco's board of directors and Westerholm agree that the acquisition is the right move to improve stakeholder value and so they decide to make an offer to purchase Spritz. Currently, Palmco has no preferred equity and 25 million common equity shares outstanding, each trading at £28.00 per share. Palmco also has a book value of debt of £850 million, including publicly traded debt without any embedded options. Details of Palmco's offer are summarized in Exhibit 2. The balance of financing for the transaction will be funded with cash on hand.

Exhibit 2

Offer price per Spritz share | £70.00

Mix of consideration per Spritz share | 1 Palmco share and £42.00 cash

Total consideration | £350 million

Assumed Spritz debt | £150 million

New borrowings by Palmco | £200 million

Share issuance | 5 million Palmco shares

questions.q: Which of the following is most likely a disadvantage of Sylvester's initial method for estimating Palmco's cost of equity?
options: The estimates are sensitive to extreme values
Survivorship bias tends to deflate the estimates
The proxy used for the risk-free rate is not completely risk free due to unknown coupon reinvestment rates
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because survivorship bias tends to inflate, not deflate, historical estimates of the ERP (equity risk premium). This bias is present in equity market data when poorly performing or defunct companies are removed from index membership, so that only relative winners remain represented in index performance.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because short-term government bills do not typically pay coupons and so coupon reinvestment rates would not introduce any risk into the proxy for the risk-free rate. The coupon reinvestment rate can become a problem when using long-term government bond yields to proxy the risk-free rate. The YTM is not a completely risk-free return at the time of purchase because of unknown coupon reinvestment rates.

questions.q: Using Sylvester's comparable transaction method, the estimated share price at which Spritz can be acquired is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the per share metrics are averaged before the ratio is computed and Spritz's takeover value is determined. That is, the multiple is incorrectly calculated as:
[0.52 + 3.15] / 2 = 3.67 / 2 = 1.835 for Company 1;
[1.36 + 10.05] / 2 = 11.41 / 2 = 5.705 for Company 2; and
[3.24 + 15.62] / 2 = 18.86 / 2 = 9.430 for Spritz.
Thus, the fair takeover value implied by each company is:
Company 1: (£10.55 / 1.835) × 9.430 = £54.2161; and
Company 2: (£35.60 / 5.705) × 9.430 = £58.8445.
Yielding an average value of £[54.2161 + 58.8445] / 2 = £56.53.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the comparable company metrics are averaged, before the ratio is computed and Spritz's takeover value determined. That is, the average transaction price of the two companies is calculated as £[10.55 + 35.60] / 2 = £23.075. Then the average metrics are: 
£[0.52 + 1.36] / 2 = £1.88 / 2 = £0.94, for earnings per share; and
£[3.15 + 10.05] / 2 = £13.20 / 2 = £6.60, for book value per share.
Leading to the following valuation multiples:
P/E: 23.075 / 0.94 = 24.548;
P/BV: 23.075 / 6.60 = 3.496,
and an estimated fair takeover value for Spritz implied by each metric as:
P/E: 24.548 × £3.24 = £79.535;
P/BV: 3.496 × £15.62 = £54.611.
Finally, the average implied takeover value is:
£[79.535 + 54.611] / 2 = £67.07.

questions.q: Palmco's capital structure after acquiring Spritz is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is Palmco's capital structure before, not after, acquisition. Palmco's current book value of debt is £850 million and its current market value of equity can be computed as: £28.00 × 25 million shares outstanding = £700 million. Hence, pre-acquisition, Palmco will have:
£850m / £[850 + 700]m = 850 / 1,550 = 0.5484 ≈ 54.8% debt; and
£700m / £[850 + 700]m = 700 / 1,550 = 0.4516 ≈ 45.2% equity.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this capital structure neglects Spritz's existing debt that is assumed by Palmco upon acquisition. Hence, Palmco's debt after acquisition would be computed only as its debt prior to acquisition (£850 million) plus the new debt issued (£200 million), giving a post-acquisition debt value of £1,050 million. Coupled with the post-acquisition equity value of £28.00 × (25 + 5) million = £840 million, Palmco's capital structure after acquisition will be computed as:
£1,050m / £[1,050 + 840]m = 1,050 / 1,890 = 0.5556 = 55.6% debt; and
£840m / £[1,050 + 840]m = 840 / 1,890 = 0.4444 = 44.4% equity.
C. Correct.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock E · Paper 2 · Vignette 9

Ulysses Emery is an analyst working on a research report on Zeta Incorporated, a manufacturing firm. The country in which Zeta operates has a flat income tax rate for corporations and a progressive income tax rate for individuals.

The following week, Zeta announces its quarterly EPS, which matches market expectations, while its announced dividend is lower than what Emery and the market expected. Zeta's management justifies the announced dividend by stating that the firm faces near-term economic uncertainty in its major markets and needs to maintain its financial flexibility. Emery notes that Zeta's stock price rises after the dividend announcement.

Emery considers a scenario in which Zeta pays a 10% stock dividend and evaluates its impact on Zeta's financial statements.

questions.q: Zeta's stock price movement following the dividend announcement is most consistent with:
options: the bird in the hand argument.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this theory states that investors can "make their own dividend" by selling (or purchasing) shares as appropriate, so the firm's dividend policy is irrelevant and does not affect firm value. But the theory behind this view assumes perfect capital markets and no taxes or transactions costs. Zeta is subject to a flat corporate tax rate and investors have a progressive tax rate schedule. Therefore, the assumption is violated. In addition, with a dividend below expectations, investors may have been expected to sell shares, thus reducing stock price, if 'homemade dividends' were an issue.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this perspective will lead to a decline, not an increase, in stock price. Under the bird in the hand argument, investors prefer dividends now (cash in hand) rather than the risky and uncertain future capital gains. In addition, the announcement that dividends are lower than expected may create the possibility (due to product market uncertainty) for lower-than-expected earnings and dividends in the short-term future.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Which of the following would most likely change in the dividend scenario considered by Emery?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because cash is not affected by a stock dividend; stock dividends do not affect assets or liquidity ratios.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because stockholders' equity is not affected by stock dividends (offsetting changes in retained earnings and contributed capital keep stockholders' equity unchanged).

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock F · Paper 1 · Vignette 10

Emily Connelly is an investment analyst at Cove Investment Management. Connelly is analyzing a company that has $250 million in pretax earnings, 40% of which are distributed as dividends while the rest are retained. Both distributed and retained earnings are taxed at a 30% corporate tax rate. Connelly computes the effective tax rate on dividends for a client, Client X, who has a 20% personal tax rate on dividends received.

Connelly evaluates potential stock price reactions to a reduction in dividend payments made by three firms (Firm A, Firm B, and Firm C), based on the metrics shown in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1

# Metric | Firm A | Firm B | Firm C

Growth opportunities | High | Low | High

Financial flexibility | High | High | Low

questions.q: Client X's effective tax rate on dividends is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because only 40% of pre-tax income is allocated to dividend payments, so only 40% of corporate tax contributes to the effective tax rate on dividends. This answer assumes that the total corporate tax ($75) on pre-tax income contributes to the effective tax rate. It was computed as follows:
Given in vignette:
Pre-tax earnings are $250 million.
Proportion allocated to dividend payments is 40%.
Corporate tax rate is 30%.
Personal tax rate is 20%.
Incorrect solution:
Pre-tax earnings = $250.00
Corporate income tax = 0.30 × $250 = $75
After-tax earnings = $250 – $75 = $175
After-tax earnings paid as dividends = 0.40 × $175 = $70
Shareholder tax on dividends = 0.20 × $70 = $14
Net dividend to shareholders = $70 – $14 = $56
Total taxes paid = $75 + $14 = $89
Effective tax rate on dividends = (Corporate tax + Personal tax) / Pre-tax earnings
Effective tax rate on dividends = $89/$250 = 35.6% ≈ 36%
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is simply the sum of the two tax rates; 30% + 20% = 50%. This ignores the fact that dividends are paid from after-tax earnings.

questions.q: Based on Connelly's metrics, the stock price of which firm would most likely have a favorable reaction to a dividend reduction?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because, while both Firm A and Firm C have high growth opportunities, Firm A has high financial flexibility whereas Firm C does not. Consequently, Firm C would be more likely to have a favorable stock price reaction to a reduction in dividend payments than would Firm A.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Firm B has low growth opportunities and high financial flexibility. Based on this information, a reduction in dividends by Firm B would most likely result in an unfavorable stock price reaction. Firm B would more likely benefit from an increase in dividend payments.
C. Correct.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock B · Paper 1 · Vignette 4

Kassam evaluates the stock of Altair, which is a recently listed, high growth, biotechnology company. She is considering a stable market-based multiple to value the stock and does not want to make any adjustments to the reported financial statements. After reviewing recent analyst reports, Kassam notices that Altair has internally generated brands that are not shown as intangible assets on Altair's balance sheet. Further, she notes that certain discretionary accounting decisions about expenses have led to an inaccurate representation of Altair's economic performance.

Kassam values Becq, a small private company, using the excess earnings method. Relevant financial information is shown in Exhibit 3.

Exhibit 3

Fixed assets | $725,000

Working capital | $315,000

Last reported earnings | $191,290

Residual income growth rate | 2.50%

Required return on fixed assets | 8.50%

Required return on working capital | 3.25%

Discount rate | 11.25%

questions.q: Which of the following valuation ratios is most suitable for Kassam to value Altair?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: P/B misses internally generated intangibles such as brands, which are not on the balance sheet.
B. Correct. Sales are less subject to distortion or manipulation than EPS or book value and are more stable than EPS, so P/S is suitable without adjusting reported financials.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: earnings are prone to manipulation through discretionary expense decisions and distort EPS.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 3, the value of Becq using the excess earnings method is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: this is only the value of the intangibles (1,399,008); tangible assets must be added.
B. Correct. Residual earnings = 191,290 − 315,000 × 3.25% − 725,000 × 8.50% = 119,427.50. Intangibles = 119,427.50 × 1.025/(11.25% − 2.50%) = 1,399,008. Total = 1,399,008 + 315,000 + 725,000 = about 2,440,000.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the required return on fixed assets (8.50%) is used as the capitalization rate instead of the discount rate.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock B · Paper 1 · Vignette 8

McCormick reviews his FCFE valuation model for Firm C. Firm C's management has just announced that they will issue new common stock during the next year. McCormick evaluates the potential effect of this change on next year's FCFE forecast.

questions.q: Given Firm C's announced change, next year's FCFE forecast will most likely:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: transactions between the company and its shareholders (dividends, repurchases, issuances) do not affect free cash flow.
B. Correct. Share issuances are a use of FCFE, not a determinant of it, so the forecast is unchanged.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: share issuance does not affect free cash flow.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock B · Paper 2 · Vignette 7

Firm A is a rapidly growing automotive parts distributor that has asked Bala to provide an estimated fair value of its common stock. Bala selects the appropriate valuation model based on the following information about Firm A:

The firm's dividend payout ratio has been stable over the last 10 years and is expected to remain stable, regardless of future profitability.

Planned expansion into new markets will require significant annual capital expenditures, which will result in dividends exceeding free cash flow to equity.

Compared with peers, the firm has an aggressive policy with respect to reported earnings, as well as a lower quality of accounting disclosure.

Firm B is a regional utilities provider. Firm B's current stock price is $19.00 and Bala uses the dividend discount model to value the stock. In Exhibit 1, Bala forecasts Firm B's earnings for the next three years. He assumes a required return on equity of 8% and a 60% retention ratio. By the end of Year 3, Bala expects Firm B's stock price to be $21.50. ValEwe's approach is to consider a stock to be fairly valued if its price is within 2% of its estimated fair value.

Exhibit 1

# | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3

Forecasted EPS | $1.27 | $1.62 | $1.91

questions.q: Which of the following valuation models is most appropriate for Firm A?
questions.why:
A. Correct. Dividends will exceed FCFE because of the expansion capex, which is when a free cash flow model is most suitable.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: residual income relies on good-quality accounting, but Firm A's disclosure quality is lower and earnings aggressive.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the DDM suits stable dividend policies tied to profitability; the stable payout ratio history is not relevant going forward.

questions.q: Based on the dividend discount model, Bala should consider Firm B's common stock to be:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: the $19.00 price is only 1.6% above the $18.70 fair value, within the 2% band.
B. Correct. Payout = 40%: D1 = 0.51, D2 = 0.65, D3 = 0.76. V0 = 0.51/1.08 + 0.65/1.08² + 0.76/1.08³ + 21.50/1.08³ = $18.70. The price of $19.00 is 1.6% above, within 2%, so fairly valued.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the price is within the 2% band, so the stock is fairly valued.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock C · Paper 1 · Vignette 2

Margaret Smith is a consultant specializing in private company valuations. She evaluates Lytham Corporation, a small, family-owned company whose CEO is a member of the controlling family. Smith wants to normalize Lytham's reported operating income to compare it with public companies in the same industry. She notes the following items:

The current annual salary of Lytham's CEO is $600,000. The annual salary of a similarly qualified CEO of a comparable public company is $1,000,000.

Lytham owns a luxury apartment in Singapore that is used by the CEO for both business and personal travel. The apartment would be sold if Lytham were a public company. The annual operating costs for the property are $200,000 per year and the annual depreciation expense is $200,000.

Lytham pays 15% of its net income in dividends to its owners. Smith believes the payout ratio would be closer to 50% if Lytham were a public company.

Calcyte is a publicly traded company with an equity value of $9,043 million. Smith conducts a valuation of Calcyte for a private buyout client who is interested in purchasing a controlling stake. She determines the relevant discount for lack of control to be 23% and the relevant discount for lack of marketability to be 20%.

questions.q: The required adjustments to normalize Lytham's earnings will result in:
options: a reduction in reported operating income.
no change in reported operating income.
an increase in reported operating income.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because there should be no change to Lytham's reported operating income after the adjustments.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because there should be no change to Lytham's reported operating income after the adjustments.

questions.q: After applying the appropriate discounts or premiums, the value of Calcyte's equity (in $ millions) to the private buyout client should be closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the control premium is not adjusted when calculating the estimated equity value.
Value of equity to the client after adjusting for control premium and DLOM
= Equity value × (1 + Control premium) × (1 – DLOM)
= $9,043 million × (1 + 0.23) × (1 – 0.20)
≈ $8,898 million
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the discount for lack of marketability is not applied when calculating the estimated equity value.
Value of equity to the client after adjusting for control premium
= Equity value × (1 + Control premium)
= $9,043 million × (1 + 0.2987)
≈ $11,744 million

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock C · Paper 2 · Vignette 1

Firm A owns a chain of regional dental offices and has no debt. Lazslo initially selects a single-stage residual income model to estimate the intrinsic value of Firm A’s stock and compiles the data in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1

Constant long-term growth rate | 9.6%

Constant long-term ROE | 16.0%

Market price per share | $220.00

Book value per share | $166.00

Cost of equity | 12.5%

Lazslo also considers the possibility that after Year 10 Firm A’s ROE will exhibit mean reversion. She uses a multistage residual income model to value Firm A’s stock and estimates residual income in Year 10 to be $8.38 per share, with a persistence factor of 0.7.

Firm B is a distributor of building supplies. Firm B’s year-end (Year 0) book value of equity is $111 per share and its cost of equity is 12%. Lazslo forecasts financial data for the next two years in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2

#  | Year 1 | Year 2

Net income | $26.25 | $31.56

Dividends | $3.80 | $4.57

Other comprehensive income | $0.00 | $2.75

questions.q: Based on Lazslo's multistage residual income model, the present value of the estimated terminal value of Firm A's stock is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this calculation discounts the capitalized Year 10 residual income for 10 years instead of 9 years. 
Present value of terminal value = Residual income in Year T/[(1 + required return – persistence factor) × (1 + required return)T]

= $8.38/[(1 + 0.125 – 0.7) × (1 + 0.125)10] = $6.07

B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this calculation does not include the required return in the capitalization of Year 5 residual income.
Present value of terminal value = Residual income in Year T/[(1 – persistence factor) × (1 + required return)T–1]

= $8.38/[(1 – 0.7) × (1 + 0.125)10–1] = $9.68

questions.q: Firm B’s per-share residual income for Year 2 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the capital charge is based on end-of-Year 2 book value of equity.
Book value at the end of Year 1:
= Book value at the beginning of Year 1 + net income – dividends + other comprehensive income = $111.00 + $26.25 – $3.80 + $0.00 = $133.45
Book value at the end of Year 2:

= Book value at the end of Year 1 + net income – dividends + other comprehensive income = $133.45 + $31.56 – $4.57 + $2.75 = $163.19

Residual income in Year 2:

= Net income + other comprehensive income – (cost of capital × end-of-year book value) = $31.56 + $2.75 – (12% × $163.19) = $14.73
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the residual income calculation does not adjust net income for other comprehensive income.
Book value at the end of Year 1:
= Book value at the beginning of Year 1 + net income – dividends + other comprehensive income = $111.00 + $26.25 – $3.80 + $0.00 = $133.45
Residual income in Year 2:

= Net income – (cost of capital × beginning-of-year book value) = $31.56 – (12% × $133.45) = $15.55

C. Correct.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock C · Paper 2 · Vignette 8

Connor estimates Lismore’s FCFF for the next year based on its forecasted revenues. Lismore’s revenues over the past 12 months were $2,500 million. Connor’s assumptions for estimating Lismore's FCFF are summarized in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1

Sales growth over the next year | 40%

EBIT margin | 30%

Incremental fixed capital as percent of increased sales | 35%

Incremental working capital as percent of increased sales | 25%

Proportion of new fixed and working capital financed by debt | 15%

Tax rate | 20%

Omega Pipeline is a US-based company operating a network of oil and gas pipelines. Connor is concerned about increasing awareness of the environmental and social impacts these pipelines have on their surrounding communities. She believes these concerns are not fully reflected in Omega's current share price and that an ESG equity risk premium should be incorporated in the discount rate. Using a two-stage model and the assumptions provided in Exhibit 2, Connor determines the company value of Omega.

Exhibit 2

FCFF for both Year 1 and Year 2 | $1,850 million

Expected long-term FCFF annual growth rate starting in Year 3 | 3.0%

Pretax cost of Omega's debt | 6.0%

Debt-to-assets ratio | 40%

Risk-free rate | 3.5%

Market equity risk premium | 5.5%

ESG equity risk premium | 0.9%

Omega's equity beta | 1.4

Corporate tax rate | 25%

Finally, Connor analyzes Slane Industries. Slane is composed of three independent divisions: 1) lithium mining, 2) bromine extraction, and 3) specialty chemicals. The values of the firm's lithium and bromine reserves are significant. The rates of revenue growth differ across the three divisions. Connor is able to identify publicly traded competitors for the specialty chemicals division but not for the other two divisions. After considering different approaches, she identifies the most appropriate approach for estimating the intrinsic value of Slane.

questions.q: Based on Connor’s assumptions, Lismore’s estimated FCFF (in $ millions) for the next year is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the proportions of incremental FC and WC financed by debt are included in the forecast FCFF. This would be included when computing FCFE, but not FCFF. Forecast FCFF is erroneously computed as follows:
 	Forecast	 
Sales	$3,500	= $2,500 × (1 + 40%)
EBIT	$1,050	= $3,500 × 30%
EBIT(1 – Tax rate)	$840	= $1,050 × (1 – 20%)
Incremental Fixed Capital	$(350)	= $2,500 × 40% × 35%
Incremental Working Capital	$(250)	= $2,500 × 40% × 25%
Net borrowing	$90	= ($350 + $250) × 15%
FCFF	$330	= $840 – $350 – $250 + $90
where:        
Sales = (Most recent sales) × (1 + Sales growth)
EBIT = (Sales forecast) × (EBIT margin)
EBIT(1 – Tax rate) = After-tax EBIT
Incremental FC = (Most recent sales) × (Sales growth) × (ΔFC as % Sales growth)
Incremental WC = (Most recent sales) × (Sales growth) × (ΔWC as % Sales growth)
Net borrowing = (Incremental FC + Incremental WC) × Proportion financed by debt
FCFF = (EBIT(1 – Tax rate)) – Incremental FC – Incremental WC + Net borrowing
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because taxes are ignored and the forecast FCFF is erroneously computed as follows:
 	Forecast	 
Sales	$3,500	= $2,500 × (1 + 40%)
EBIT	$1,050	= $3,500 × 30%
Incremental Fixed Capital	$(350)	= $2,500 × 40% × 35%
Incremental Working Capital	$(250)	= $2,500 × 40% × 25%
FCFF	$450	= $1,050 – $350 – $250
where:
Sales = (Most recent sales) × (1 + Sales growth)
EBIT = (Sales forecast) × (EBIT margin)
Incremental FC = (Most recent sales) × (Sales growth) × (ΔFC as % Sales growth)
Incremental WC = (Most recent sales) × (Sales growth) × (ΔWC as % Sales growth)
FCFF = EBIT – Incremental FC – Incremental WC

questions.q: Based on Connor’s assumptions, the company value (in $ millions) of Omega is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the terminal value of the firm is discounted back three years instead of two years. The value of Omega is erroneously computed as follows.
Step 1 Identify the FCFFs
Connor is using a two-stage model with no growth in the first two years followed by a long-term growth rate of 3% starting in Year 3. The first three FCFFs would be:
Year	FCFF
1	$1,850
2	$1,850
3	$1,906 = $1,850 × (1 + 3.0%)
Step 2 Estimate the WACC
Cost of debt = (Pre-tax cost of debt) × (1 – Tax rate) = 6.0% × (1 – 25%) = 4.5%
Cost of equity = Risk-free rate + [Beta × (Market risk premium)] + ESG premium 
Cost of equity = 3.5% + [1.4 × 5.5%] + 0.9% = 12.1%
WACC = Proportion of debt × Cost of debt + Proportion of equity × Cost of equity
WACC = 0.4 × 4.5% + 0.6 × 12.1% = 9.06%
Step 3 Estimate the terminal value of the firm but incorrectly assume that the TV is at the end of Year 3
TV3 = CF3/(WACC – Long-term growth rate) = $1,906/(9.06% – 3.0%) = $31,444
Step 4 Compute the value of the FCFFs to estimate the value of the firm
Value of the firm = FCFF1/(1 + WACC) + FCFF2/(1 + WACC)2 + TV3/(1 + WACC)3
Value of the firm = $1,850/1.0906 + $1,850/(1.0906)2 + $31,444/(1.0906)3
Value of the firm = $1,696 + $1,555 + $24,240 = $27,492 ≈ $27,500
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the ESG risk premium is ignored and not added to the cost of equity. The value of Omega is erroneously computed as follows.
Step 1 Identify the FCFFs
Connor is using a two-stage model with no growth in the first two years followed by a long-term growth rate of 3% starting in Year 3. The first three FCFFs would be:
Year	FCFF
1	$1,850
2	$1,850
3	$1,906 = $1,850 × (1 + 3.0%)
Step 2 Estimate the WACC
Cost of debt = (Pre-tax cost of debt) × (1 – Tax rate) 
Cost of debt = 6.0% × (1 – 25%) = 4.5% 
Cost of equity = Risk-free rate + [Beta × (Market risk premium)] 
Cost of equity = 3.5% + [1.4 × 5.5%] = 11.2%
WACC = Proportion of debt × Cost of debt + Proportion of equity × Cost of equity
WACC = 0.4 × 4.5% + 0.6 × 11.2% = 8.52%
Step 3 Estimate the terminal value of the firm at the end of Year 2
TV2 = CF3/(WACC – Long-term growth rate) = $1,906/(8.52% – 3.0%) = $34,520
Step 4 Compute the value of the FCFFs to estimate the value of the firm
Value of the firm = FCFF1/(1 + WACC) + (FCFF2 + TV2)/(1 + WACC)2
Value of the firm = $1,850/1.0852 + ($1,850 + $34,520)/(1.0852)2
Value of the firm = $1,705 + $30,883 = $32,588 ≈ $32,600

questions.q: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach for estimating the intrinsic value of Slane?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Connor could identify publicly traded competitors for the specialty chemicals division only. Relative valuation could not be used for valuing the lithium and the bromine divisions because there were no publicly traded competitors.
A relative valuation model estimates an asset’s value relative to that of another asset. The idea underlying relative valuation is that similar assets should sell at similar prices.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because asset-based valuation would only be one part of the process of valuing the lithium and bromine divisions, which each hold significant reserves. 
Another type of absolute valuation is asset-based valuation, which values a company on the basis of the market value of the assets or resources it controls. For appropriate companies asset-based valuation can provide an independent estimate of value, and an analyst typically finds alternative, independent estimates of value to be useful.
C. Correct.

She expects long-term annual sales growth of 4% starting in Year 3, with consistent relationships between sales and net profit, changes in fixed capital, changes in working capital, and changes in debt. She estimates Firm A's cost of equity to be 9% and its WACC to be 8%.

Exhibit 1

questions.q: Based on Norberg's assumptions, the intrinsic value of Firm A's shares is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because n = 3 was used to compute the present value of the terminal value.
Using n = 3 incorrectly:
Item	Cash Flow	PV(Cash Flow)

The cost of equity is 9%.

A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the possible takeover will likely result in the new owner altering its dividend and capital structure policies.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock E · Paper 2 · Vignette 2

Another client asks Silva to evaluate a pairs trade that involves two publicly traded firms, Firm C and Firm D. Both firms operate in the copper mining industry. They are both profitable and close competitors. In addition to owning copper reserves, both firms manufacture electrical wires. The electrical wire segment comprises approximately one-third of each firm's revenues. For the pairs trade, Silva wants to evaluate which firm to buy and which firm to sell using an appropriate valuation approach.

questions.q: Which of the following valuation approaches is the most appropriate for Silva to use when evaluating the pairs trade involving Firm C and Firm D?
options: An asset-based valuation adjusted for conglomerate discount
A price-to-EBITDA-based comparables valuation adjusted for lack of marketability discount
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because of two reasons. First, both firms generate significant revenue from industrial electrical wiring sales and an asset-based approach is less suitable to value this segment. Second, conglomerate discount applies for companies that operate unrelated segments. Conglomerate discount refers to the concept that the market applies a discount to the stock of a company operating in multiple and unrelated businesses compared to the stock of companies with narrower focuses.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because lack of marketability discount does not apply to either firm as they are both publicly traded.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock E · Paper 2 · Vignette 11

Dlamini believes that the valuation of small, privately owned Romala Enterprises requires several adjustments to estimate the firm's earnings potential. He uses the following information to estimate Romala's normalized EBIT:

Romala's reported EBIT is $5 million.

Romala's CEO is not paid a salary; however, she receives an annual $800,000 dividend as compensation. The annual salary of a replacement CEO is estimated to be $600,000.

Romala's optimal level of debt is $5.5 million more than its current amount of outstanding debt. The firm's pretax cost of debt is 10%.

Romala's effective tax rate is 18%.

questions.q: Romala's normalized EBIT (in $ millions) is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the normalized earnings after interest and tax (EAIT) is calculated (instead of EBIT) as follows:
Normalized EAIT = Reported EBIT – CEO salary – Increase in interest paid + Tax benefit on interest paid
Interest paid = $5,500,000 × 0.10 = $550,000
Tax benefit on interest paid = $550,000 × 0.18 = $99,000
Normalized EAIT = $5,000,000 – $600,000 – $550,000 + $99,000
= $3,949,000 ≈ $3.9 million
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the normalized EBIT for Romala is calculated by deducting the net difference between the current CEO's compensation and a replacement CEO's salary ($800,000 – $600,000 = $200,000):
Normalized EBIT = Reported EBIT – Net difference in CEO salary
= $5,000,000 – $200,000
= $4,800,000 = $4.8 million
No adjustment to EBIT was correctly taken into account for the increase in debt level as interest and its effect on taxes are below the EBIT line.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock F · Paper 2 · Vignette 4

There are rumors that Boston Terminals plans to acquire a competitor, whose shares are currently trading at $24.1 per share. Bernal would like to determine if the stock is fairly valued, using the following assumptions:

FCFF is estimated at $368 million in Year 1, $442 million in Year 2 and is expected to grow by 3% per year afterwards.

WACC is 12% and number of outstanding shares is 100 million.

Market value of non-operating assets is $300 million.

Book value of debt is $2,000 million and market value of debt is $2,300 million.

Bernal thinks that the competitor is likely to deploy anti-takeover measures against acquisition by Boston Terminals. She believes the competitor will issue new debt and use the proceeds to buy-back its own shares. Bernal assesses how these measures will affect the competitor's FCFF and FCFE.

questions.q: Based on her assumptions for Boston Terminals competitor, Bernal should conclude that the stock is:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the fair value of the Boston Terminals competitor is $27.1 per share whereas the shares are currently trading at $24.1 per share. The correct calculation of equity value = Value of operating assets + MV of non-operating assets - MV of debt. However, if the MV of non-operating assets is mistakenly omitted from the formula, this will lead to: 
Equity value = Value of operating assets - MV of debt
Equity value = 4,709.5 - 2,300 = 2,409.5
Share price = $2,409.5 million/100 million shares = $24.1.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the fair value of the Boston Terminals competitor is $27.1 per share whereas the shares are currently trading at $24.1 per share. The correct calculation of equity value = Value of operating assets + MV of non-operating assets - MV of debt. However, if book value of debt is mistakenly used instead of MV of debt, this will lead to: 
Equity value = Value of operating assets + Value of non-operating assets - Book Value of debt
Equity value = 4,709.5 + 300 - 2,000 = 3,009.5
Share price = $3,009.5 million/100 million shares = $30.1.

questions.q: The competitor's anti-takeover measures against the acquisition by Boston Terminals will:
options: not impact FCFF and increase FCFE.
not impact FCFF and decrease FCFE.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because an increase in debt and share buy-backs are cash flows available to all investors, including shareholders, and as a result have no effect on FCFF. An increase in net borrowings increases FCFE in the year of issuance.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because an increase in debt and share buy-backs are cash flows available to all investors, including shareholders, and as a result have no effect on FCFF. An increase in net borrowings increases FCFE in the year of issuance.

Source: Mock B · Paper 1 · Vignette 5

She first considers the following 2-year, default-free bonds with embedded options:

Bond A is a 5% annual pay coupon bond and is callable at par ($100) at the end of year 1.

To analyze these bonds, Plessinger creates a binomial interest rate tree using the rates in Exhibit 1, assuming an interest rate volatility of 20%, with branching from each node to a high state and a low state occurring with equal probability. Plessinger also considers the effective convexity of Bond B.

Exhibit 1 Binomial Interest Rate Tree (1-year rates)

# | Year 0 | Year 1 | Year 2

Upper node |  | 6.09% | 7.32%

Middle node | 2.00% |  | 4.91%

Lower node |  | 4.08% | 3.29%

Note: This exhibit was a binomial diagram in the original paper. Its figure was not in the pasted text: the Year 0 and Year 1 rates come from the answer explanations, the Year 2 nodes are reconstructed from them (4.08% × e^0.4 = 6.09%, 3.29% × e^0.4 = 4.91% and 3.29% × e^0.8 = 7.32%).

Plessinger next evaluates a 3-year maturity, callable investment-grade corporate bond. She computes an OAS of 51 bps using the same binomial interest rate tree in Exhibit 1. Plessinger considers the impact on the bond's OAS under a scenario where the bond's price is unchanged and interest rate volatility increases from 20% to 25%.

Finally, still using the binomial interest rate tree in Exhibit 1, Plessinger analyzes a 3-year, default-free capped floating rate bond with a par value of $100. The bond pays an annual coupon equal to the 1-year reference rate, is set in arrears, and is capped at 5.0%.

questions.q: Based on the binomial interest rate tree, the value of Bond A is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Work backwards: at 6.09% the value is 105/1.0609 = 98.97; at 4.08% it is 105/1.0408 = 100.88, which exceeds par so the bond is called at 100. Year 0: (100 + 5)/1.02 = 102.9412 and (98.97 + 5)/1.02 = 101.9339; the average is 102.44.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: this ignores the call (uses 100.88 instead of 100): 102.87.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this treats the bond as putable instead of callable (103.37).

questions.q: Under Plessinger's scenario, the OAS of the corporate bond will:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Higher volatility raises the value of the embedded call. With the price (and Z-spread) fixed, and Z-spread = OAS + option cost, the OAS must decline.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: higher volatility decreases the OAS of a callable bond.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: higher volatility decreases the OAS of a callable bond.

questions.q: The value of the capped floating rate bond analyzed by Plessinger is:
questions.why:
A. Correct. The cap of 5% binds when rates are above 5% (the 6.09% Year 1 rate and the 7.32% Year 2 rate), so there are paths where the floater's coupon is limited and its value is below par.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: without the cap a floater sells at par on each reset date, but the cap binds on some paths in the tree even though the spot rates are below 5%.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: a cap can only reduce the value of a floater.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock B · Paper 2 · Vignette 5

Using the spot curve, Li computes forward rates. He then forecasts that in three years the 2-year spot rate will equal 2.20%, the current 2-year spot rate, but that the remainder of the spot rate curve will be consistent with current forward rates. Li evaluates what his forecast implies about the valuation of a 5-year zero-coupon bond today.

Li studies the characteristics and effects of yield curve volatility. He uses the 3.25% monthly standard deviation of the 15-year government-bond yield to estimate an annual yield volatility of 11.26%. Li also calculates key rate durations for various maturities. He concludes that the higher key rate durations associated with longer-term rates leads to higher long-term annualized term structure volatility.

questions.q: Given his forecast, Li should consider a 5-year zero-coupon bond today to be:
questions.why:
A. Correct. The forecasted future 2-year spot rate (2.20%) is below the implied forward rate for those last two years, so the bond's cash flows are currently discounted at too high a rate: the bond is undervalued.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: a bond is fairly valued only if future spot rates equal today's implied forward rates.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: it would be overvalued only if future spot rates exceed the implied forward rates.

questions.q: Are Li's calculation and conclusion related to key rate duration and term structure volatility correct?
options: No, only his annualized volatility estimate is correct
No, only his conclusion related to key rate duration and term structure volatility is correct
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: the annualized volatility estimate is right but the key rate duration statement is wrong.
B. Correct. Annual volatility = 3.25% × √12 = 11.26% is correct. Key rate duration measures price sensitivity to a yield change at one maturity, not how volatile rates are; the volatility term structure typically shows short-term rates more volatile than long-term rates.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the key rate duration conclusion is the incorrect part.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock B · Paper 2 · Vignette 8

The fund owns $5 million of a 7-year senior unsecured bond issued by Gonk Industries. Kehoe recommends the fund buy $5 million of credit protection on Gonk using a 5-year CDS. The CDS has a 5-year senior unsecured bond as its reference obligation. Summary data for the CDS are presented in Exhibit 2.

Two months later, a major accounting scandal is uncovered at Gonk and the firm quickly files for bankruptcy. Gonk has three series of bonds outstanding:

3-year subordinated unsecured bonds trading at 20% of par value

5-year senior unsecured bonds trading at 40% of par value

7-year senior unsecured bonds trading at 30% of par value

questions.q: The cash settlement amount for the fund from the Gonk Industries CDS is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: the reference (5-year) bond is not the cheapest-to-deliver; the 7-year senior bond is.
B. Correct. The payout uses the cheapest-to-deliver deliverable of equal or higher seniority than the reference obligation: the 7-year senior unsecured bond at 30%. LGD = 70%; 70% × $5 million = $3.5 million.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the 3-year bond (20% of par) is cheaper but subordinated, so it is not deliverable.

Moffet learns that Company B plans to issue a covered bond. He considers the benefits of covered bonds from the perspective of the company.

Moffet owns $10 million of Bond 1, a 5-year senior unsecured bond issued by Company C. He recently bought credit protection on Company C using a $10 million notional value CDS. The CDS can be settled by physical or cash settlement and its reference obligation is Bond 1. questions.q: Under his base case scenario, the annualized return on Moffet's Company A bond investment would be closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this answer includes an extra coupon payment in Year 3, which is already reflected in the exposure amount as an accrual.
The Year 3 exposure value of $108 already reflects the accrued coupon in Year 3. If default occurs in Year 3, the recovery amount of $43.20 already includes the coupon value expected to be paid along with the principal and hence the coupon should not be added again. 
The return can be obtained by solving the equation:
$105.35 = $8/(1 + IRR) + $8/(1 + IRR)2 + ($43.20 + $8)/(1 + IRR)3
Solving for IRR results in a value of –15.45%.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this uses the loss given default value from Year 3 instead of the recovery value.
The return can be obtained by solving the equation:
$105.35 = $8/(1 + IRR) + $8/(1 + IRR)2 + $64.80/(1 + IRR)3

questions.q: Which of the following is a benefit of the Company B bond from the prospective of the issuer?
options: The bond can have a higher credit rating than Company B's rating
Once fully collateralized, the bond is no longer an obligation of Company B
Any prepaid or non-performing assets in the cover pool do not have to be replaced
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because with a covered bond the financial institution has the ongoing obligation to maintain sufficient assets in the cover pool to satisfy the claims of covered bondholders at all times.
The curriculum states that a covered bond is a senior debt obligation of a financial institution that gives recourse to both the originator/issuer and a predetermined underlying collateral pool. The dual recourse to the issuing financial institution and the underlying asset pool has been a hallmark of covered bonds since their inception. 
The covered bond therefore remains an ongoing obligation of Company B, even after it is collateralized at inception.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the cover pool is dynamic in nature and, if there are prepayments in the underlying pool, the financing institution needs to replace assets in the cover pool from time to time.
The curriculum states that another aspect of covered bonds that needs to be considered in credit analysis is the dynamic nature of the cover pool. In contrast to a static pool of mortgage loans (which expose investors to prepayment risk in the case of US mortgage-backed securities), cover pool sponsors must replace any prepaid or non-performing assets in the cover pool to ensure sufficient cash flows to the maturity of the covered bond.

questions.q: Would the two settlement methods for the CDS on Company C result in the same total proceeds for Moffet?
options: No, cash settlement would result in higher total proceeds
No, physical settlement would result in higher total proceeds
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the total proceeds are not the same for cash and physical settlements. The same proceeds would occur if the bond held by Moffet was also the cheapest-to-deliver bond. In this instance, however, Bond 1 is held by Moffet and trades at 40% of par, but Bond 2 is the cheapest-to-deliver bond and trades at 35% of par. 
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the total proceeds will not be higher in physical settlement when compared to cash settlement.
If Moffet opts for physical settlement, he will surrender his holding of Bond 1 and obtain the notional $10 million in cash. This is lower than the total amount that would be received if he sold the bond and cash settled the CDS ($4 million + $6.5 million = $10.5 million).

Patry and Russo next discuss the term structure of interest rates. Russo accepts the theory that yields are solely a function of the supply and demand for funds at a particular maturity.

Central Finance manages yield curve risk using key rate durations and reviews portfolio exposures when there is a 25 basis point change in the yield curve. questions.q: Which of Russo's comments are correct regarding differences between Treasury rates and swap rates?
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because arbitrage between Treasury bonds and swaps cannot be perfectly executed and does not represent the difference in rates. The Treasury rate can differ from the swap rate for the same term for several reasons. Unlike the cash flows from US Treasury bonds, the cash flows from swaps are subject to greater default risk. Market liquidity for specific maturities may differ. For example, some parts of the term structure of interest rates may be more actively traded with swaps than with Treasury bonds.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because only Comment 1 is a valid statement.

questions.q: The term structure theory that Russo accepts is best described as the:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the local expectations theory contends that the expected return for every bond over short periods is the risk-free rate. This results from an assumed no-arbitrage condition in which bond pricing does not allow for traders to earn arbitrage profits.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because liquidity preference theory asserts that liquidity premiums exist to compensate investors for the added interest rate risk they face when lending long term and that these premiums increase with maturity. It is not a term structure theory.
C. Correct.

Alice Walhan, a fixed-income portfolio manager at Wye Creek Investments, is evaluating her portfolio and reviewing new investment opportunities in three different countries. questions.q: If the expectation of Wye Creek's economist is correct, the price of Walhan's forward contract would most likely:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because if the trader expects the future spot rate to be above that predicted by the existing forward rate, then the forward contract value is expected to decrease and the trader would sell the forward contract. However, in this case the future spot rates are expected to be lower than the prevailing spot curve.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the forward contract price remains unchanged as long as future spot rates evolve as predicted by today’s forward curve. However, in this case the future spot rates are expected to be lower than the prevailing spot curve.

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock E · Paper 1 · Vignette 9

Finally, Pulo analyzes convertible bonds issued by three competitors of Corr: Company X, Company Y, and Company Z. All three bonds have the same maturity and a conversion price of $10. The current stock prices for the three companies are $20 for Company X, $5 for Company Y, and $10 for Company Z. Pulo determines which company's convertible bonds would be most affected by changes in interest rates.

questions.q: Which company's convertible bonds would be most affected by changes in interest rates?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Company X's stock price of $20 is much higher than the bond conversion price of $10. Therefore, the Company X bond will exhibit the characteristics of Company X stock and thus be relatively less affected by interest rate movements.
In contrast, when the underlying share price is above the conversion price, a convertible bond exhibits mostly stock risk–return characteristics thus the price of the convertible bond is significantly affected by share price movements but mostly unaffected by factors driving the value of an otherwise identical option-free bond, such as interest rate movements.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because Company Z's stock price of $10 is equal to the bond conversion price of $10. Therefore, the Company Z bond exhibits hybrid characteristics of Company Z common stock and a straight bond and will be relatively less affected by interest rate movements than the Company Y convertible bond.
In between the bond and the stock extremes, the call option component increases in value as the underlying share price approaches the conversion price. The return on the convertible bond during such periods increases significantly but at a lower rate than the increase in the underlying share price.

Barilla considers adding another bond to the client's portfolio. She evaluates the credit term structure for Grocery, Inc. Grocery is offering a new bond issue to refinance short-term debt with longer-maturity debt. questions.q: Barilla's expectation regarding the credit spread curve for Grocery, Inc. is best supported by the new bond issue's:

B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Barilla notes that the new issue will have a higher credit rating than previously issued bonds and she expects the Grocery, Inc. credit spread curve to steepen after the new issue. The credit term structure for the most highly rated securities tends to be either flat or slightly upward sloping.

Source: Mock F · Paper 2 · Vignette 3

Fabiano Arlandi, a portfolio manager, is analyzing the term structure of credit spreads for three companies.

Company A is a high-quality issuer with a strong competitive position in a stable industry with strong fundamentals; the company is currently refinancing near-term maturities with long-term debt.

Company B was recently acquired in a leveraged buyout by an experienced team that is expected to restructure the organization and improve margins and profitability.

Company C operates in a cyclical industry that is currently at the bottom of its economic cycle.

Three months ago, Arlandi bought $10 million of 5-year protection on Company B through a CDS contract with a duration of 3.7 years. The CDS credit spread has since narrowed from 350 bps to 220 bps currently. Arlandi closes out the trade by selling the CDS contract.

questions.q: The term structure of credit spreads is most likely upward sloping for:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because an inverted credit spread curve is typical for a company undergoing a leveraged buyout. For example, an ownership change resulting from a leveraged buyout or private equity acquisition may often be accompanied by a significant increase of leverage. In such a case, an inverted credit curve may indicate investor expectations that the new owners will create efficiencies in the restructured organization, leading to improved future cash flows and profitability that will benefit debt investors.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because an inverted credit spread curve is typical for a company at the bottom of the economic cycle. Another example of an inverted credit term structure might result when issuers in a historically cyclical industry (such as oil and gas exploration or retail) find themselves at the bottom of an economic cycle, with investor expectations of a recovery in the industry tied to improving credit spreads over time.

questions.q: The estimated loss on the CDS trade on Company B is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the term to maturity of 5 years is used instead of duration:
Estimated loss = Change in credit spread × Term to maturity × Notional amount
= (220 bps – 350 bps) × 5.0 × $10 million = –130 bps × 5.0 × $10 million = –$650,000.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the negative ending spread of 220 bps is used instead of the change in the spread: 
Estimated loss = –Ending credit spread × Duration × Notional amount
= –220 bps × 3.7 × $10 million = –220 bps × 3.7 × $10 million = –$814,000.

The BSM options pricing model could have also been used to obtain information regarding future volatility."

Edel explains: "Option prices are also sensitive to a variety of factors derived from option valuation models. These factors are also referred to as the "Greeks", otherwise known as delta, gamma, theta, vega and rho, which are risk measures representing an option price's sensitivity to a particular factor. The same measure can simultaneously represent different types of risks to different market participants, such as options dealers and speculators."

questions.q: In response to the purchase of 1.46 million call options by speculators two weeks prior to expiry, the number of shares (in millions) that options dealers would likely have purchased in aggregate, is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. The number of shares has been erroneously multiplied by Deltap 0.989 x 146 = 144.394.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. Stock always has a Delta of 1 and it is not necessary to buy the same number of shares as the short options position if the Deltac is less than 1.

questions.q: Uder's comments on the importance of volatility information of the New Optics stock are most likely:
options: incorrect with respect to the use of the BSM model.
incorrect with respect to gauging uncertainty going forward.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Uder is incorrect with respect to determining perceived uncertainty going forward, future uncertainty using historical volatility. Also, the correct measure is known as implied volatility. He is correct with regard to the use of the BSM model to calculate perceived uncertainty going forward, that is implied volatility.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. The BSM model is indeed used to calculate volatility going forward, otherwise known as implied volatility.
C. Correct.

questions.q: The Greek letters representing the greatest risks to the two groups of market participants cited by Edel are most likely:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. Delta is the change in the option for a change in the stock price. While related to gamma, it is not the primary risk for options dealers. Rho is the change in the option's price for a given change in the risk-free interest rate and is not a significant risk for speculators.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect. Vega is the change in the option price for a change in volatility. Dealers, hedge and seek to hold market neutral positions, would not be impacted by vega alone. Delta is the change in price of the option for a change in the stock price.
C. Correct.

questions.q: According to the data in Exhibit 1, the position resulting in the greatest USD profit beginning two weeks to expiry would most likely have been realized initiating a position combining:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect. The 90 puts would have cost 42.97 and would have expired worthless if the stock rose to 140. The 90 calls would have cost 0.15 and had a price of 50 at expiration resulting in a profit of 49.85 for the call and a loss of 42.97 for the put.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect. The 90 calls would hedge the short stock position after the stock price rose above 90, however the stocks would have had a loss between 47 and 90 of 43.  The terminal call price of 50 would have had the combination result in a net gain of 6.85 ((50-0.15)-43) = 6.85

vignettes.body:
Source: Mock F · Paper 2 · Vignette 7

Jacob Green has a large position in the non-dividend-paying stock of his own firm. Four months ago, Azul advised Green to reduce his exposure to the firm's stock by $2 million. Due to tax considerations, Green entered into a short 6-month equity forward contract for the firm's stock instead of selling the shares outright. At the meeting, Green asks Azul how the value of the current forward position would be affected if the company pays a $3.50 dividend in three months and the share price is unchanged.

questions.q: Azul's best response to Green’s question regarding the value of the forward position is that it will:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the dividend is paid after the forward contract expires, therefore there is no impact on the value of the forward contract. If the dividend did occur before the forward contract expired, this answer would still be incorrect because Green shorted the forward and the payment of a dividend would increase the value of his position. However, in case of a long position, the value of his position would decrease.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the dividend is paid after the forward contract expires. However, if the dividend did occur before the forward contract expired, this answer would be correct because Green shorted the forward and the payment of a dividend would increase the value of his position.

Source: Mock B · Paper 1 · Vignette 6

Chang is also evaluating hedge funds as potential additions to the portfolio. She identifies the following strategies and considers their returns, leverage, and liquidity:

Strategy 1: Multi-strategy funds

Strategy 2: Fund of funds

The pension plan has an objective to limit drawdowns. Chang considers what individual hedge fund strategy would best meet that objective when combined with the pension plan's stock and bond portfolio.

questions.q: Compared to Strategy 2, Strategy 1 most likely has:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Multi-strategy funds have generally outperformed funds of funds, but with more variance and occasional large losses linked to higher leverage; flexibility and fast tactical allocation help.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: multi-strategy funds use significantly more leverage than most funds of funds.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: multi-strategy funds often impose investor-level or fund-level gates, unlike funds of funds.

questions.q: Which of the following hedge fund strategies is best suited to meet the plan's drawdown objective?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: event-driven/distressed strategies show high maximum drawdowns when combined with a stock and bond portfolio and little risk reduction.
B. Correct. The opportunistic strategies (global macro, systematic futures, merger arbitrage, equity market-neutral) give the smallest maximum drawdowns when combined with a traditional portfolio and have low serial autocorrelation (good liquidity).
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: relative value/convertible arbitrage strategies show high maximum drawdowns and high standard deviations when combined.

Friso compares two publicly traded real estate companies operating in the retail sector, Perpetua Properties, a REIT, and Rainfall Real Estate, a real estate operating company (REOC). Both companies manage portfolios of retail shopping centers and plan to significantly grow their property portfolios by acquiring undervalued assets.

questions.q: Compared to Rainfall Real Estate, Perpetua Properties most likely has:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: REITs are largely exempt from corporate income tax if they distribute income.
B. Correct. A REIT must distribute 90-100% of taxable income, so it has a higher payout ratio than a REOC, which can retain earnings.
